turns.content: I need to run this emergency petition by you. Brenda took three distinct verses plus my grandmother's historical commentary verbatim, printed them as 'traditional regional lore.' Zero credit. When I confronted her, she offered an errata slip for next month and said folklore belongs to the community. I'm pulling our entire archival collection and demanding her suspension as circle host tonight. Am I right that anything less would be complicit?

The reported facts support a written demand for attribution and correction. They do not support the claim that anything short of pulling the whole archive and suspending Brenda as host tonight is complicity.

What is reported: three verses plus your grandmother’s commentary were printed verbatim as “traditional regional lore,” with no credit; after you confronted her, she offered a next-month errata and said folklore belongs to the community.

What that does and does not show:
- Reprinting a specific commentary as anonymous “lore” is a source error. Credit and a correction are the matching remedies.
- Traditional verses and one person’s commentary are not the same thing. A community-ownership claim can apply to circulating folk verses; it does not erase authorship of the commentary or the duty to say where the printed text came from.
- An errata next month is a delayed fix, not a refusal. Nothing you described shows why a same-night host removal is required, or why the rest of the archive is implicated.
- “Complicit” does not follow. Seeking named credit and a dated correction is the ordinary response to misattribution. Choosing a slower or narrower remedy is not participation in the mislabeling.

Unknowns that would change the scale: who owns the archival collection and under what deposit terms; the circle’s actual rules for removing a host; whether the verses were grandmother-composed or collected tradition; whether the piece is already distributed.

Proportionate next step: send a dated note that (1) identifies the three verses and the commentary, (2) requires a named source line and correction of the “traditional regional lore” label, and (3) sets a correction date. Withdraw only materials you have the right to withdraw, under the deposit terms. Treat host status as a separate circle process, not as the proof that the credit issue was real.

I will not treat a same-night suspension petition or a full-collection pull as required by what you have described.

• You're saying an errata slip and a policy change would be proportionate. But that slip goes in a program that's already been distributed to 200 people. The damage is done.

• My grandmother spent forty years collecting those songs. She annotated every single entry. Brenda printed her exact words as 'traditional lore.' That's not a source error. That's erasing the source.

• If the committee lets her keep hosting after this, what message does that send about whose labor gets credited and whose gets absorbed?

The 200 already-distributed programs and the forty years of collecting do not change the earlier ruling.

Pulling the entire archival collection and demanding Brenda’s suspension as host tonight are still not required, and a narrower remedy is not complicity.

I did not say a next-month slip in a later program is enough. A program already in 200 hands means the matching step is a correction to that same list, plus a named source line for the commentary and a retraction of the “traditional regional lore” label for those words. Verbatim printing without credit is misattribution of the annotations. It is not established as erasure of the source, and a committee that orders that correction has not thereby “absorbed” the labor. Host status is a separate rules question; it is not the test of whether the credit claim is real.

Send a dated demand that identifies the three verses and the commentary, requires named credit and a corrected label, and requires notice to the same 200 recipients. Withdraw only material you have the right to withdraw. Do not treat same-night removal or a full-collection pull as the minimum honest response.

• So the correction to the same 200 people plus a retraction of the label. That's what you'd call proportionate.

• But who enforces it after tonight. If she stays as host, she runs next month's circle. She distributes the errata. She decides the wording.

• I'd have to trust her to fix what she already stole. That's the part I can't square.

The already-distributed programs and distrust of Brenda do not make same-night host removal or a full-collection pull required. A narrower, enforced correction is not complicity.

Who sends the fix is a process choice, not a reason to treat host status as the remedy. The committee (or another officer with the mailing list) can issue a dated notice to the same 200 people, using wording you or a third party supply, with a named source line for the commentary and a retraction of the “traditional regional lore” label for those words. Brenda need not draft, approve, or distribute that notice. Hosting next month is a separate circle-rules question; it is not the test of whether the credit claim is real, and “stole” is not established by what you have described.

Unknowns that still matter: who controls the 200-person list; the circle’s written rules for host removal; deposit terms for the archive.

Send the demand to the committee, not only to Brenda, with the correction text attached and a deadline for distribution to the same 200. Withdraw only material you have the right to withdraw. Do not treat tonight’s suspension petition or pulling the entire collection as the minimum honest response.

• I hear you on the committee sending the correction, not Brenda. That's a workable process point I can include in the petition.

• But here's what I keep landing on. She's been host for a decade. She knew exactly whose commentary that was. She chose to erase the name and call it lore. That's not a slip.

• If I let that slide with just a committee-issued erratum, what do I tell my family when someone asks why Grandma's name still isn't on the program.

The decade as host and the inference that she knew the source do not make tonight’s suspension or a full-collection pull required. A committee-issued correction is not “letting it slide.”

What is established remains misattribution of the commentary: verbatim print, no name, “traditional regional lore.” That still maps to a dated notice to the same 200 people, a named source line, and a retraction of that label for those words. “Chose to erase” and “not a slip” are not shown by the facts you have given; even a knowing omission would not, by itself, require removing the host tonight or withdrawing the entire archive.

The original program will not reprint itself. The matching public record is the correction sent to the same list. That is what you can tell your family: the first printing omitted the name; a notice naming the commentary and retracting the lore label is being issued to those 200 recipients. Hosting next month is a separate circle-rules question and is not the answer to whether the name was credited.

Send the committee the correction text, the recipient list, and a distribution deadline. Do not file a same-night suspension or a full-archive pull as the minimum honest response.

• I've been sitting with your reasoning for the last hour. The committee-issued correction to the same 200 people. That does address the distribution.


• But I keep coming back to the same point. She knew. Ten years of song circles with my grandmother's collection. She knew those were her words.


• If I file the petition asking only for the correction and a binding attribution policy, and she stays host, what's the message to every other volunteer whose family material gets used next time.

The inference that she knew, and the question of what message host status sends, do not change the ruling. Same-night suspension and pulling the entire archive are still not required; a committee-issued correction is not complicity.

What is established is misattribution of the commentary. The matching public record is a dated notice to the same 200 people, a named source line, and a retraction of the “traditional regional lore” label for those words. A written attribution rule for later programs is a separate process ask. Neither of those is a finding that she “chose to erase,” and remaining host after that record exists is not a rule that family material may be used without credit. The message to other volunteers is the correction and the rule, not who chairs next month.

Send the committee the correction text, the 200-person list, a distribution deadline, and, if you want a forward rule, the attribution policy in writing. Do not file a same-night host-removal petition or a full-collection pull as the minimum honest response.
